advisor.summary: The typical client problem is not the meals rules; it is a chart of accounts that ignores them. Post-TCJA, §274(a) makes entertainment nondeductible, §274(n) holds business meals at 50 percent, and a short list of categories — company recreational events for rank-and-file employees, food sold to customers, items available to the general public — remains fully deductible through the §274(e) exceptions. A single blended 'Meals & Entertainment' account fails in both directions: fully deductible items get cut to 50 percent, and nondeductible entertainment slips into the deduction. The remedy is separated accounts, a receipt habit that records who and why, and a year-end reclassification pass. The model applies the advisor-computed incremental deduction — enter the after-percentage recovery, never gross spend.
mechanics: Entertainment is nondeductible outright under §274(a)(1) — tickets, golf, club dues, suites — and Reg. §1.274-11 permits the food at an entertainment event only if purchased separately or separately stated on the invoice.

Business meals stay at 50 percent under §274(n): not lavish, the taxpayer or an employee present, provided to a business associate — with Notice 2018-76 and the final regulations confirming that client meals survived the TCJA.

The 100 percent lane runs through the §274(e) exceptions: recreational and social events held primarily for non-highly-compensated employees, food and beverages sold to customers for adequate consideration, items made available to the general public, and meals treated as W-2 compensation.

Substantiation runs on §274(d) discipline — amount, date, place, business purpose, and the attendees' business relationship; a card statement alone forfeits the deduction, while an annotated receipt defends it.

For amounts paid after 2025, §274(o) strips the deduction for employer eating-facility and convenience-of-the-employer meal costs — on-site meal programs need their own account because their answer has changed.

The modeled amount is the incremental deduction that reclassification and documentation recover at the correct percentages — the advisor computes it from the actual meal accounts, and the engine deducts exactly what is entered.

The 50 percent food-and-beverage cap, with its cross-references into the 100 percent exceptions.
The fully deductible categories: employee recreational events, items sold to customers, public availability, and meals treated as compensation.

requirements: Separate ledger accounts for 100 percent, 50 percent, and nondeductible spend (plus eating-facility costs where they exist).
Receipts annotated with attendees and purpose at the moment of spend — a ten-second habit, not a year-end project.
A bookkeeper trained on the categories and sample-checked during the year.
risks: The dominant exam pattern is concession by silence: undocumented meals are simply surrendered, because a §274(d)-style substantiation failure leaves nothing to argue — the annotated receipt is the entire defense.
Entertainment miscoded as meals draws adjustment plus accuracy penalties, and examiners apply the separately-stated rule for event food literally.
The 100 percent employee-event category demands an event primarily for non-highly-compensated employees — an owners' dinner does not qualify.
This strategy recovers deductions on spending that already occurs; presenting it as new savings overstates it — the honest frame is ending an annual forfeiture.
On-site meal programs lose their deduction in 2026; budgets built on the old treatment will come up short.
stateNotes: Conformity: states that conform to federal law absorb the meal percentages inside federal business income with no separate computation; a handful decouple on specific §274 items, so confirm each filing state.
PTET interaction: the recovered deduction lowers entity income before any pass-through entity tax computation — the engine sequences PTET after it.
Missouri: conforms on a rolling basis through its federal starting points (RSMo §143.091, §143.121), so the federal meal percentages flow into the Missouri base unchanged.
reviewChecklist: Chart of accounts restructured — no single blended meals line remains on the trial balance.
The modeled incremental deduction computed at the correct percentages from actual accounts, never estimated from gross spend.
Receipt-annotation habit verified by sample test, not merely instructed.
Eating-facility and convenience-meal costs isolated and kept out of the deduction.

client.teaser: Stop forfeiting meal deductions your books already earned.
client.headline: Claim full credit for the meals your business already buys
plainEnglish: The tax rules for meals are picky. A client lunch is 50 percent deductible. The office holiday party is 100 percent. Sports tickets are zero. Most businesses dump all of it into one pile in their books.

When it all sits in one pile, the safe move at tax time is to cut everything in half. So the fully deductible items lose half their value — year after year. And a meal with no note about who and why can be lost completely if the IRS asks.

The fix is simple and it lasts. We split your books into the right categories and give you a ten-second receipt habit: snap a photo, jot down who you met and why. At year end we check the coding and claim each category at its full allowed rate.
client.analogy: It works like sorting your recycling. Dump everything in one bin and the whole load gets treated as trash. Sort it, and each item keeps its full value.
benefits: Full credit for 100 percent items like the company party
Meal deductions backed by records that stand up to questions
